Chapter Seven: The Bell Beneath the Salt

P01 The tide had gone out before sunrise, and Ilsa walked the flats with her chart rolled under one arm and her boots heavy with grey mud.

P02 Somewhere ahead, under a mile of shallow water and silt, the drowned bell of Corrow was said to ring whenever a liar crossed the marsh.

P03 She did not believe the story, but she had been paid to map the old causeway, and the causeway ran straight past the sunken tower.

P04 A heron with wings like frosted glass followed her at a careful distance, stepping between the reeds as if it were counting her footprints.

P05 "You are not a very subtle guide," Ilsa told it. The heron tilted its head and said nothing, which she supposed was fair.

P06 By midmorning the fog thinned enough to show the first stones of the causeway, green with weed and set in a line too straight to be natural.

P07 She knelt, measured the width of the road with a knotted cord, and wrote the number in the margin of her chart with a stub of charcoal.

P08 The stones were warm. Not sun-warm, which would have made sense, but warm from below, like a hearth that someone had banked for the night.

P09 Ilsa pressed her palm flat against the rock and felt, faint and slow, a vibration that rose and fell like a held breath.

P10 The heron stepped closer. Its glass feathers caught the light and scattered small rainbows across the mud between them.

P11 "If you know what is down there," she said, "now would be a good moment to share." The bird preened one wing and looked away.

P12 She followed the causeway east. Every hundred paces she stopped, measured, and marked the chart, and every hundred paces the warmth grew stronger.

P13 At noon she found a carved marker half buried in silt. The letters were worn almost smooth, but she could still trace the shape of a bell.

P14 Beneath the bell was a line of script she did not recognise, angular and patient, cut by someone who had expected it to outlast them.

P15 She copied the script into her notebook stroke by stroke, then sat back on her heels and drank the last of the water from her flask.

P16 The marsh was very quiet. Even the gulls had gone inland, and the only sound was the slow tick of water draining through the reeds.

P17 Then, from far below her feet, came a single low note, so deep that she felt it in her teeth before she heard it with her ears.

P18 Ilsa stood very still. She had told no lies that morning, unless she counted the one she had told herself about not believing the story.

P19 The heron spread its wings. For a moment it looked less like a bird and more like a window, and through it she saw the marsh as it had once been.

P20 There were houses on stilts, and lanterns strung between them, and a tall white tower rising from a square of clean dry stone.

P21 People moved along the causeway carrying baskets of eels and bundles of reed. None of them looked up; none of them could see her.

P22 At the top of the tower hung the bell, bronze and enormous, and a child sat on the ledge beside it swinging her bare feet over the drop.

P23 The vision folded closed as the heron lowered its wings. The houses were gone, and the marsh was only mud and reeds and grey sky again.

P24 Ilsa realised she had dropped her charcoal. She found it in the silt, wiped it on her sleeve, and drew the tower on her chart where it had stood.

P25 "That was a gift," she said to the heron, "or a warning. I would appreciate knowing which." The bird blinked its pale eyes slowly.

P26 She walked on until the causeway ended at a ring of broken pillars, each one leaning outward as though something had pushed up from the centre.

P27 In the middle of the ring the mud was soft and dark, and a thin thread of steam rose from it into the cooling afternoon air.

P28 Ilsa tied her cord to the nearest pillar and lowered a weighted line into the soft ground. It sank, and sank, and did not find a bottom.

P29 When she drew the line back up, the brass weight was polished bright, as if it had been scrubbed clean by many careful hands.

P30 The tide was turning. She could hear it now, a soft rush far out on the flats, and she knew she had perhaps an hour before the road went under.

P31 She marked the ring on her chart, wrote the depth as unknown, and underlined the word twice so that no one who read it later could mistake it.

P32 The heron walked to the edge of the soft mud and looked back at her, then down at the steam, then back at her again, plainly waiting.

P33 "No," Ilsa said. "I map things. I do not climb into them." The heron made a sound that was almost, but not quite, a laugh.

P34 She turned toward the shore. Behind her the bell rang a second time, softer now, and the note followed her all the way back along the causeway.

P35 By the time she reached the dunes the water had covered the stones, and only the tops of the broken pillars showed above the incoming tide.

P36 She sat on the sand and unrolled the chart. In the margin, beside the tower she had drawn, someone had added a small bell in fine brown ink.

P37 It was not her handwriting. It was not anyone's handwriting she knew, and the ink was still slightly wet when she touched it with her fingertip.

P38 Far out over the water, a shape with glass wings rose into the evening and turned once above the place where the tower had stood.

P39 Ilsa rolled the chart up, tied it with the knotted cord, and decided that the people who had paid her could hear about the bell in person.

P40 Then she walked inland toward the lights of the village, and did not look back, though she felt the marsh watching her the whole way.
